The discussions of the British-Russian Committee, which met in Paris a fortnight ago to promote Trade Union unity and to facilitate the entry of Russia into the Amsterdam International, were far from harmonious, according to a report by M. Andreev, Chairman of the Soviet delegation to the Central Council of Soviet Labour Unions.

M. Andreev says that, the British delegation, consisting of representatives of the Council of the Trade Union Congress, refused to discuss the question of assistance to the British miners, "which had been placed on the agenda for their approval. They also demanded that the Russians should withdraw a resolution condemning the conduct of the Trade Union' Congress in the general strike. The Russians refused to do so, and declared that the Russian Labour Union would continue to support the miners.
Reuter
The petition of the Knights of Columbus for diplomatic intervention on the Méxicoan religious controversy and the repeal of the embargo on the import of arms has been presented to Mr. Kellogg.
Higher Columbus officials conferred on the matter with Mr. Kellogg for some time, but the discussion was strictly private.
Mr. Kellogg is going to-morrow to President Coolidge's Summer camp, where, it is expected, the whole Mexican situation will be discussed. — Reuter's American Service.
The War Department officially denies that priests were executed anywhere in Mexico. It describes the reported encounters between soldiers and Catholics as exaggerated.
The American Ambassador to Mexico is leaving for two months' vacation in the United States.—Reuter.

According to the papers, the last phase of the parley between metallurgists of France, Germany, Belgium and Luxembourg, for the formation of an Iron Trust, began yesterday. Le Matin foresees the signing of an agreement to-morrow.—Havas.

Negotiations of the great Continental Trusts, in which representatives of heavy metal industries in France, Germany, Belgium, and Luxembourg are concerned, are reaching their final stages in Paris. The British position is stated at present to be rather obscure, although the "Westminster Gazette" learns on high authority that the British steel interests do not intend to enter into the combine.—Reuter.

Le Journal says that it is most improbable that British industrialists will attempt to attack the trust; as it is already a member of the rails combine. It further expresses the opinion that it is awaiting the reply of the American manufacturers, who are certain to take up the challenge of the new trust, which will likely organise effectually against American dumping.

FRENCHMAN WHO THREWA STONE.

The Commissioner of Police at Granville has concluded an inquiry into the stone-throwing of July 26, "when a lady" passenger was seriously injured by a Frenchman who threw a stone.
Interrogated the Frenchman said that he and others on the quay strongly resented passengers throwing coppers. He deep-
ly repented of the stone-throwing and humbly apologised to the injured lady and the other passengers.

The Commissioner Severely Re-primanded him.—Reuter.
[A cable of July 26 states: Excursionists from "Jersey to Granville have had an unpleasant experience." On leaving Granville the steamer band struck up the "Marseillaise." The crowd on the quay resented this and started throwing stones. A woman passenger was hit. Much indignation prevails in Jersey over the incident. Granville is a small town in the Department of Manche, in France.]

Chang Tsung-chang's first division of Shantung troops, commanded by Hsieh Yu-hsien, while en route to Nankow from Shantung, mutinied this morning between Langfang and Laofa; and held up this morning's train to Tienisin at the latter point.—Reuter.
Official reports state that one Shantung regiment mutined early this morning.
Other Shantung troops were hurried to the scene by the brigade commander and most of the mutineers were subdued and disarmed. Some escaped soon after the outbreak.
No reason is given for the mutiny, which was suppressed by eleven o'clock, after which the train service was resumed.— Reuter.
